prompt: Two students each take a separate SRS of $100$ students from the same school and ask whether they bring lunch from home. One gets $58$ percent "yes"; the other gets $64$ percent. What best explains the difference?

choices.label: At least one of the samples must have been biased
Sampling variability: different random samples naturally give different statistics
The population proportion changed between the two samples
A sample of $100$ is too small to produce a meaningful percent

hint: A sample statistic is NOT the population parameter. Each new random sample gives a slightly different number.

hints.text: A sample statistic is NOT the population parameter. Each new random sample gives a slightly different number.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: flip a fair coin 10 times twice. You might get 4 heads, then 6 heads. Neither coin is unfair; that is just chance. Same thing with samples of students.
Both samples were random, so bias is not the natural explanation. What word describes chance differences from sample to sample?
The difference is ordinary sampling variability: choice B.

explanation: Both are proper SRSs from the same population, so both are unbiased. Unbiased does not mean exact.
Each sample of $100$ catches a different mix of students by chance, so the sample percent bounces around the true value. A gap of $6$ points between two samples of $100$ is very ordinary.
This chance-to-chance variation is sampling variability. Choice B.

alternativeExplanations.title: How much bounce to expect
steps: For a proportion near 0.6 with $n = 100$, the typical sample-to-sample spread is about $\sqrt{\frac{0.6 \cdot 0.4}{100}} \approx 0.05$, or 5 points.
So 58 and 64 are each about one of those steps from a true value near 61 percent.
Later units turn this into a standard error and a margin of error.

alternativeExplanations.title: Bias vs variability
steps: Bias is a consistent lean in one direction caused by the method; random sampling removes it.
Variability is scatter from sample to sample; larger samples shrink it but never erase it.
Here the method is fine, so what remains is variability, not bias.
